en.title: BE FAST: how to spot a stroke
en.summary: Six quick checks that tell you a stroke may be happening, and why every minute counts.
en.body:
A stroke happens when blood stops reaching part of the brain. The sooner the person gets to hospital, the more of the brain can be saved.

Use BE FAST to check:

B - Balance: sudden loss of balance, dizziness or trouble walking.
E - Eyes: sudden loss of sight in one or both eyes, or double vision.
F - Face: one side of the face drops. Ask them to smile.
A - Arms: they cannot lift both arms and keep them up. One arm drifts down or feels weak or numb.
S - Speech: words are slurred or muddled, or they cannot speak or understand you.
T - Time: get emergency help straight away. Use the Emergency button at the top of this app.

Other sudden signs can include a very bad headache unlike any before, confusion, or numbness down one side of the body.

If the signs go away within minutes or hours, still get help the same day. This can be a mini-stroke (TIA), and it is a warning that a bigger stroke may follow.

en.title: While you wait for help
en.summary: What to do, and what not to do, in the minutes before the ambulance or transport arrives.
en.body:
Once you have called for help:

- Note the time the signs started, or the last time the person was seen well. Doctors need this to choose treatment.
- Stay with the person and keep them calm.
- If they are drowsy or being sick, lay them on their side so they can breathe.
- Loosen tight clothing around the neck.
- Gather their medicines, or a list of them, to take to the hospital.

Do not:

- Give food or drink. Swallowing may not be safe.
- Give any medicine, including aspirin. Some strokes are caused by bleeding, and aspirin can make them worse.
- Wait to see if the signs go away.
- Let the person drive themselves.

en.title: The first weeks: what to expect
en.summary: Recovery is often fastest early on. Here is what usually happens and how to help it along.
en.body:
Every stroke is different, and so is every recovery. Many people improve most in the first weeks and months, and some keep improving for years.

In hospital, the team will usually:
- Check whether swallowing is safe before giving food or drink.
- Start medicines to lower the chance of another stroke.
- Begin rehabilitation: help with moving, speaking, everyday tasks and feelings.

In the first weeks it is common to:
- Feel very tired, even after small tasks.
- Have ups and downs in mood.
- Find some things easier on some days than others.

What helps:
- Practise the exercises your team shows you, a little and often.
- Ask questions. Write them down before appointments; the My visit page in this app can hold them.
- Rest when you need to. Tiredness is part of healing.

en.title: Coming home from hospital
en.summary: A checklist for the move from hospital to home.
en.body:
Before leaving hospital, ask:
- Which medicines to take, when, and for how long.
- When and where the next check-up is.
- Which exercises to keep doing, and how often.
- Who to contact if you have a question.

At home:
- Clear paths of loose mats, cables and clutter to prevent falls.
- Put things you use every day within easy reach.
- Use a light at night between the bed and the toilet.
- Keep a list of your medicines and bring it to every appointment.

It is normal to find the first days at home tiring or worrying. Tell your health worker how you are getting on, including how you feel.

en.title: Why blood pressure matters
en.summary: High blood pressure is the biggest cause of stroke you can do something about.
en.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your blood vessels. When it stays high for a long time, it damages the vessels, including those in the brain.

High blood pressure usually has no signs. Many people feel completely well. The only way to know is to measure it.

A reading has two numbers:
- The top number is the pressure when the heart beats.
- The bottom number is the pressure when the heart rests between beats.

Your health worker will tell you what your own numbers mean and what to aim for.

What helps keep blood pressure down:
- Taking blood pressure medicines every day, even when you feel fine.
- Eating less salt.
- Being active, not smoking, and drinking little or no alcohol.

Never stop or change a medicine on your own. Talk to your health worker first.

en.title: Measuring blood pressure at home
en.summary: Simple steps for a reading you can trust.
en.body:
Before you measure:
- Do not smoke, exercise or have a hot drink for half an hour.
- Empty your bladder.
- Sit with your back supported and feet flat on the floor for five minutes. Do not cross your legs.

When you measure:
- Rest your arm on a table so the cuff is level with your heart.
- Put the cuff on bare skin, not over a sleeve.
- Stay still and do not talk.
- Take two readings, one minute apart.

Afterwards:
- Write both numbers down straight away, or add them in the Blood pressure page of this app.
- Measure at about the same times each day, as your health worker suggests.

If a reading worries you, or you feel unwell, contact your health worker. If you have any stroke signs, use the Emergency button.

en.title: Taking your medicines safely
en.summary: Medicines after a stroke lower the chance of another one, but only if they are taken every day.
en.body:
After a stroke, people are often given medicines to:
- Lower blood pressure.
- Stop blood clots forming.
- Lower cholesterol.

Tips:
- Take them at the same time every day. Linking them to a daily habit, like breakfast, helps.
- Use a pill box with a space for each day.
- Mark each dose in the Medicines page of this app, so you and your carer can see what has been taken.
- Keep taking them even when you feel well.

If you miss a dose, check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist. Do not take two doses to make up.

If you take a medicine that thins the blood, tell your health worker about unusual bruising or bleeding.

Always tell any doctor, nurse or pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including herbal or traditional remedies.

Remember:
- Take two readings a minute apart.

en.title: Moving safely at home
en.summary: Practice helps the brain relearn movement. Here is how to do it safely.
en.body:
After a stroke, the brain can form new connections. Repeating movements, a little and often, helps it relearn.

- Do the exercises your physiotherapist or health worker gave you. Ask them to check you are doing them right.
- Short sessions several times a day are better than one long one.
- Have someone nearby when you practise standing or walking, until you are steady.
- Wear well-fitting shoes with a good grip.
- Use any walking aid you were given.

Stop and rest if you feel dizzy, short of breath or in pain. Get emergency help for chest pain or any new stroke signs.

Log your movement in the Movement page of this app. It helps your team see how you are getting on.

en.title: Everyday tasks are practice too
en.summary: Washing, dressing and eating are good practice when done safely.
en.body:
Everyday tasks use the same skills as exercises. With your team's advice:

- Try to use your weaker arm or hand in simple tasks, like holding a cup with both hands or wiping a table.
- Dress sitting down. Put the weaker arm or leg in first, and take it out last.
- Break tasks into small steps and take your time.

For carers: it can be quicker to do things for the person, but letting them do what they safely can helps their recovery. Offer help when it is asked for, or when safety needs it.

en.title: What is aphasia?
en.summary: Many people find speaking, understanding, reading or writing harder after a stroke.
en.body:
Aphasia is a problem with language caused by damage to the brain. It does not affect intelligence. The person still knows what they want to say.

Someone with aphasia may:
- Struggle to find the right word.
- Use the wrong word, or words that do not make sense.
- Find it hard to follow fast or long conversations.
- Have trouble reading, writing or with numbers.

Speech and language therapy can help. Many people keep improving for a long time.

Other speech problems can happen too, such as slurred speech when the muscles used for talking are weak.

The Talk page in this app has picture tiles that speak common words aloud.

en.title: Tips for talking together
en.summary: Small changes that make conversations easier for everyone.
en.body:
- Find a quiet place. Turn off the radio or TV.
- Face the person and speak a little more slowly, in short sentences.
- Ask one question at a time. Questions with a yes or no answer are easier.
- Give plenty of time to answer. Do not rush or finish their sentences unless they ask.
- Use gestures, pictures, writing or pointing as well as words.
- Check you have understood: "Do you mean...?"
- Speak to them as the adult they are, and include them in conversations.

It is normal for both of you to feel frustrated sometimes. Take a break and try again later.

en.title: Swallowing problems after a stroke
en.summary: Signs to watch for, and why following the advice on food and drink matters.
en.body:
A stroke can weaken the muscles used for swallowing. This is called dysphagia. Food or drink can go into the lungs and cause a chest infection.

Watch for:
- Coughing or choking when eating or drinking.
- A wet or gurgly voice after swallowing.
- Food left in the mouth, or taking a long time to eat.
- Repeated chest infections, or a high temperature.

If you notice these, tell your health worker.

A speech and language therapist may advise softer foods or thicker drinks. Follow this advice exactly, even if the person asks for something different, until the therapist changes it.

en.title: Safer mealtimes
en.summary: Simple habits that make eating and drinking safer.
en.body:
- Sit fully upright, in a chair if possible.
- Take small mouthfuls and small sips, one at a time.
- Eat slowly. Swallow fully before the next mouthful.
- Avoid talking while chewing, and turn off distractions.
- Stay upright for at least half an hour after eating.
- Keep the mouth clean: brush teeth or dentures twice a day. Food left in the mouth can cause infections.

Medicines: ask a pharmacist before crushing tablets or opening capsules. Some must not be crushed.

If the person chokes and cannot breathe, cough or speak, get emergency help straight away.

en.title: Caring day to day
en.summary: Practical ways to support someone at home after a stroke.
en.body:
- Keep a simple daily routine: medicines, meals, exercises and rest at the same times.
- Encourage the person to do what they safely can. It helps recovery and confidence.
- Help them practise the exercises from their team.
- Make the home safe: clear floors, good lighting, grab rails if possible.
- Keep track of medicines and appointments. This app can show you doses marked and upcoming visits.
- Write down questions and changes you notice, to share at appointments.

Know the stroke signs (BE FAST). A second stroke is most likely in the first weeks and months. If you see any sign, get emergency help straight away.

en.title: Looking after yourself as a carer
en.summary: Caring is hard work. Your health matters too.
en.body:
Many carers feel tired, worried or low, especially in the first months. This is common.

- Rest when you can, and try to keep your own sleep and meals regular.
- Share tasks with family, friends or neighbours. Make a list of things others could help with.
- Keep some time for things you enjoy.
- Talk about how you feel, with someone you trust or with a health worker.
- Look for a local support group for stroke survivors and carers.

If you feel you cannot cope, tell a health worker. Asking for help is part of caring well.

en.title: Feelings after a stroke
en.summary: Changes in mood are common after a stroke, and help is available.
en.body:
A stroke can change how a person feels, both because of the damage to the brain and because life has changed.

Common feelings include:
- Sadness, low mood or losing interest in things (depression).
- Worry or fear, including fear of another stroke (anxiety).
- Crying or laughing suddenly, without feeling that way inside (emotionalism).
- Frustration and anger.

These are not a sign of weakness. Talk to your health worker about them. Talking therapies, support groups and sometimes medicines can help.

You can note how you feel in your daily check-in.

If you, or the person you care for, have thoughts of self-harm or of not wanting to live, get help straight away using the Emergency button.

en.title: Managing tiredness
en.summary: Extreme tiredness (fatigue) is one of the most common effects of a stroke.
en.body:
Fatigue after a stroke is more than normal tiredness. It may not get better with rest, and can come on suddenly.

What helps:
- Plan your day. Do the most important things when you have most energy.
- Break tasks into small parts and rest between them.
- Keep a regular sleep routine.
- Gentle activity, built up slowly, can improve energy over time.
- Tell family and friends, so they understand when you need to stop.

Tell your health worker if tiredness does not improve or gets worse. Other things, such as low mood, poor sleep or some medicines, can add to it.

en.title: Preventing a stroke: the main steps
en.summary: Most strokes are linked to things you can change. Here are the ones that matter most.
en.body:
Whether you want to prevent a first stroke or another one, the same steps help:

- Keep blood pressure under control. Check it regularly and take any medicines every day.
- Eat less salt and more fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains.
- Be active most days.
- Do not smoke, and avoid other people's smoke.
- Drink little or no alcohol.
- Keep diabetes and cholesterol under control, if you have them.
- Get an irregular heartbeat checked. It can cause clots that lead to a stroke.
- Keep a healthy weight.

You do not have to change everything at once. Pick one step, start small, and build from there. Each step in this section has its own page.

en.title: Cut down on salt
en.summary: Too much salt raises blood pressure. The WHO advises less than five grams a day, about one teaspoon.
en.body:
Most of the salt we eat is already in food: stock cubes, processed and packaged foods, bread, sauces and snacks.

The World Health Organization advises adults to eat less than five grams of salt a day in total. That is just under one level teaspoon, including the salt already in food.

Ways to cut down:
- Cook with less salt and fewer stock cubes. Add flavour with herbs, spices, garlic, onion, ginger or lemon.
- Taste food before adding salt at the table, or remove the salt shaker.
- Eat fewer salty snacks and processed meats.
- Choose fresh foods over packaged ones when you can.

Your taste changes. After a few weeks, food with less salt starts to taste normal.

en.title: Eat for a healthy heart and brain
en.summary: Simple changes to everyday meals that lower the risk of stroke.
en.body:
- Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit. Aim for at least five portions a day.
- Choose beans, lentils, nuts and whole grains often.
- Use small amounts of vegetable oils rather than butter, lard or palm oil.
- Eat less fried food, processed meat and sugary drinks.
- Limit added sugar and salt.
- Drink water instead of sweet drinks.

If you have diabetes, a swallowing problem or another condition, ask your health worker which foods are right for you.

en.title: Stay active
en.summary: Regular activity lowers blood pressure and the risk of stroke.
en.body:
The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least two and a half hours of moderate activity a week. That is about half an hour on five days. Moderate means you breathe faster but can still talk.

Any activity counts: walking, gardening, housework, dancing, cycling.

- Start slowly and build up. Even ten minutes at a time helps.
- Sit less. Get up and move every hour if you can.

After a stroke, ask your health worker or physiotherapist what is safe for you before starting something new.

You can record your activity in the Movement page of this app.

en.title: Stop smoking
en.summary: Smoking damages blood vessels and makes clots more likely. Stopping helps at any age.
en.body:
Tobacco in any form, including cigarettes, chewing tobacco and shisha, raises the risk of stroke. Breathing other people's smoke does too.

The risk starts to fall soon after you stop, and keeps falling over the years.

Tips:
- Choose a day to stop, and tell family and friends.
- Remove cigarettes, lighters and ashtrays from home.
- Notice what makes you want to smoke, and plan something else to do then.
- Ask a health worker about support and medicines that help people stop.

If you slip, do not give up. Many people need several tries.

en.title: Alcohol and stroke
en.summary: Drinking alcohol raises blood pressure and the risk of stroke. Less is better.
en.body:
Alcohol raises blood pressure and can cause an irregular heartbeat, both of which make a stroke more likely. Heavy drinking at one time is especially risky.

The World Health Organization says there is no safe level of drinking for health.

- If you do not drink, do not start.
- If you drink, cut down, and have several alcohol-free days each week.
- Alcohol can react with some medicines. Ask your health worker or pharmacist.

en.title: Diabetes and stroke
en.summary: High blood sugar over time damages blood vessels. Keeping it under control lowers stroke risk.
en.body:
Diabetes means the body cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood. Over time, high blood sugar damages blood vessels, including those in the brain.

Signs can include being very thirsty, passing urine often, tiredness and blurred vision. Many people have no signs. A simple blood test can tell.

If you have diabetes:
- Take your medicines as advised.
- Eat regular, balanced meals and stay active.
- Go to your check-ups, and keep your blood pressure under control too.

en.title: Irregular heartbeat and stroke
en.summary: Atrial fibrillation can cause clots that travel to the brain. Treatment lowers the risk.
en.body:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a heart rhythm problem. The heart beats irregularly and often fast. Blood can pool in the heart and form clots, which may travel to the brain and cause a stroke.

Some people notice a fluttering or pounding heartbeat, breathlessness, dizziness or tiredness. Others have no signs.

- If your pulse often feels irregular, see a health worker. A simple heart tracing can check for AF.
- If you have AF, you may be offered medicine to prevent clots. Take it exactly as advised.
